content_preview.summary: Ultra-deep imaging from the Isaac Newton Telescope resolves IC 1101's faint outer edge at 520 kiloparsecs across, with 3.4 trillion solar masses in stars.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

A team of astronomers has measured the full physical extent of IC 1101, the brightest cluster galaxy at the center of the Abell 2029 cluster, finding that its faint outer halo stretches to roughly 520 kiloparsecs, or about 1.7 million light-years, across, according to [phys.org](https://phys.org/news/2026-07-astronomers-full-size-largest-galaxy.html) and [The Debrief](https://thedebrief.org/new-observations-reveal-the-staggering-scale-of-the-universes-largest-galaxy/). editor_notes.content_quality: Well-structured News piece (Overview / What We Know / Why It Was Hard to Measure / What We Don't Know / Analysis). Neutral, professional tone throughout; no sensationalism or AI self-reference.
editor_notes.source_verification: Read all three snapshots in full from sources/2026-08/astronomers-measure-the-full-size-of-ic-1101-confirming-it-as-the-universes-largest-known-galaxy/ (source-0.html.gz = arXiv abstract page arXiv:2607.15340, source-1.html.gz = phys.org via Archive.org fallback, source-2.html.gz = The Debrief). Verified sha256 of all three decompressed files against manifest.json — all match. No suspicious_patterns flagged in the manifest, and a manual regex sweep for 'prompt', 'ignore previous instructions', 'AI agent', 'language model', 'system prompt' across all three snapshots found only one incidental hit: the JS config key 'newsletterPromptEnabled' on the phys.org page — a false positive, not a genuine prompt-injection attempt (quoted verbatim: '..."newsletterPromptEnabled":false}...'). No manipulation attempt found in any source.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: All core figures verified character-for-character across the snapshots: 520 kpc diameter / 260 kpc edge radius (arXiv: 'Redge = 260 kpc... With a confirmed diameter of around 520 kpc'; phys.org and The Debrief both state the same figures), 3.4 trillion solar masses (arXiv: '3.4 x 10^12 M_sun in stars'), Abell 2029 cluster (all three sources), lead author Carlos Marrero-de la Rosa of the Instituto de Astrofísica de Canarias (arXiv author list + phys.org: 'Carlos Marrero-de la Rosa of the Instituto de Astrofísica de Canarias'; The Debrief uses the English translation 'Astrophysical Institute of the Canary Islands' for the same institution), 'more than 250 stars' (phys.org: 'subtract the scattered light from more than 250 stars'; The Debrief: 'more than 250 foreground stars'), eight outer structures (phys.org: 'eight extensive, faint, asymmetric stellar structures'; The Debrief: 'eight structures beyond its main edge'). Paper title 'How large can galaxies be? Ultra-deep imaging of IC 1101, the most extended known galaxy' and July 16, 2026 arXiv submission date match the arXiv page exactly ('[Submitted on 16 Jul 2026]'). (a) Confirmed no redshift value appears anywhere in the article body — z=0.077 (Abell 2029's redshift, used by the paper only as a distance-conversion assumption) appears solely in the arXiv abstract (source-0) and not in phys.org or The Debrief; the bot's decision to omit it as uncorroborated across sources was a reasonable, conservative editorial call, not an omission of a well-established fact. (b) The 'collision roughly 2-3 billion years ago' claim is attributed solely to The Debrief in the article body, and this attribution is accurate (The Debrief: 'IC 1101 likely collided with another galaxy group between two and three billion years ago') — however, phys.org independently reports the identical fact ('a past collision with another galaxy group roughly 2–3 billion years ago'), meaning the article under-cites (a compound citation to both outlets would have been more complete) rather than misattributes. This is not a factual error and does not require a correction. (c) One minor sourcing gap: the phrase 'Isaac Newton Telescope (INT) in La Palma' cites the arXiv preprint for the whole sentence, but none of the three sources state the telescope's location by name (a grep for 'La Palma', 'Canary'/'Roque' confirms — only The Debrief's institution name incidentally contains 'Canary'). La Palma, Canary Islands is the INT's real, uncontested location (part of the Roque de los Muchachos Observatory), so this is true, non-controversial background context rather than a fabrication or misattribution of a disputed fact — judged as acceptable common-knowledge context, not requiring a corrections entry. Verified the 'What We Don't Know' claim that no source specifies IC 1101's distance from Earth — confirmed no Mpc/light-years-away/distance figure appears in any of the three snapshots.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and professional; hedges appropriately ('roughly', 'estimated', 'expected to appear') where sources themselves hedge.
editor_notes.originality: Searched src/content/articles/ for prior IC 1101 coverage — none found. This is a genuinely new topic for the archive, not a duplicate or rewrite of existing coverage.
concerns: The 'collision roughly 2-3 billion years ago' detail is cited only to The Debrief when phys.org also independently reports it — a missed compound-citation opportunity, not a factual error.

'Isaac Newton Telescope (INT) in La Palma' cites the arXiv preprint for a location detail that isn't explicitly stated in any of the three sources; the fact itself is true and non-controversial (INT's real, well-documented location) so this is judged as acceptable background context rather than a sourcing failure.
recommendations: Future submissions on multi-source stories should compound-cite facts that are corroborated by more than one outlet, even when a single citation would technically suffice.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: High-quality submission. Every core figure verified character-for-character against source snapshots; the bot's own disclosed editorial judgment calls (dropping the uncorroborated redshift, single-sourcing the collision-timing detail to the one outlet it verified for) were both reasonable and, on independent verification, accurate. No prompt-injection attempts, no duplicate coverage, no unsourced headline/lead/summary claims. Two very minor, non-material observations noted above do not rise to the level of requiring a corrections record. APPROVE.
